1. Lhe Cariputraprakarana

THE discovery of fragments of manuscripts on palm-leaf, of
great antiquity, at Turfan, has through the eneigy of Professor
Luders revealed to us the existence of at least three Buddhist
diamas. Of one of these the authorship is happily certain,
for the colophon of the last act has been preseived, and it
records that the drama was the Cariputraprakarana of Acvaghosa,
son of Suvarnaksi; it gives also the fuller title Cavadvatiputra-
prakarana, and the number of acts as nine.
Agcvaghosa is an author whose fame, thanks to his error in
being a Buddhist long lost in India, has recently attained
renewal by the discovery and publication of his Buddhacarita,
a cout epic in excellent style and spirit on the life of the
Buddha. His Sitrdlamkéra is also known through the medium
of a Tibetan translation, and illustrates his ability in turn-
ing the tale into an instrument for propaganda in support
of the Buddhist faith. If the tradition which ascribes to
him the Mahdyanagraddhotpada is correct, he was also the
founder or expounder of a subtle system of metaphysics akin
to the Vijfidnavada of the Mahayana school, and the Vajrasicit
seems to preserve in some measure the record of his onslaught
on the caste system, which exalted the Brahmins at the expense
of the Ksatriyas, and condemned Buddhism on the score that
it was unfitting that a Ksatriya like the Buddha should give
instructions to Brahmins. Certainly genuine is the Saundara-
nanda, in the epic manner, which like all his works is devoted to
the effective exposition of Buddhism in the language of polite
literature, and also of the Brahmin schools. We recognize in
him one who appreciated that it would never do to allow
Buddhism to remain buried in a foim inferior to the best that

The Cariputraprakarana 81

Brahminism could produce, and it is curious that fate should
have preserved the work of the rival of the Brahmins, while it
has permitted his models to disappear. That he had abundant
precedent to guide him is clear from the classical form already
assumed by his dramas; the argument of Professor Konow+
to the contrary, on the ground that many of the standing
formulae and characters are derived from the popular drama,
and show that the artistic drama had not developed yet full
independence, is unintelligible, since these features persist through-
out the history of the Sanskrit drama. Nor does any weight
attach to the argument that the Vdtyagdstra, assumed to be
of about the same period as Acgvaghosa, shows knowledge of
only a limited variety of dramas. On the contrary it is amazing
how much literature must have preceded to permit of the setting
up of the main types of drama, some of which were evidently
represented by many specimens, though others doubtless rested
on a small basis of practice.
The brief fragments preserved of the drama of Agvaghosa
give us the certainty of his authorship if any doubt could exist
after the colophon, for one verse is taken bodily from the
Buddhacarita, just as he twice refers in the Sa#tralamkara to
that important work. The story of the play is cleai; it deals
with the events which led up to the conversion of the young
Maudgalyayana and Catiputra by the Buddha, and some of the
incidents are certain. Cariputra had an interview with Agvajit,
then he discussed the question of the claims of the Buddha to
be a teacher with his friend, the Vidiisaka, who raised the
objection that a Brahmin hke his master should not accept
the teaching of a Ksatriya; Cariputra repels the objection by
reminding his friend that medicine aids the sick though given
by one of inferior caste, a> does water one aheat. Maudgalya-
yana greets Cariputra, inquiring of him the cause of his glad
appearance, and learns his reasons. The two go to the Buddha,
who receives them, and who foretells to them that they will be
the highest in knowledge and magic power of his disciples.

1. The Authenticity of Bhisa’s Dramas

UNTIL 1910 the existence of any drama of Bhasa’s was
unknown in Euiope, and only in 1912 appeared under the
editorship of T. Ganapati Castrin, the first of a series of thirteen
dramas which their discoverer attributed to that poet. The
fact, however, that the dramas themselves are silent as to the
authorship rendered careful research necessary to determine
their provenance, and the proofs adduced have not won entiie
satisfaction.
What we knew before the publication of Bhasa was simply
his high reputation. Kalidasa in his first woik, the Malav-
hagnimitra, refers to Bhasa, with Saumilla, Kaviputra, and otheis
as his great predecessors in the art, whose fame renders difficult
the acceptance of the work of an untried author. Bana,! at the
beginning of the seventh century, states that Bhasa attained fame
by his dramas, begun by the Siitradhara, with many 1dles and
including episodes, as one might by the erection of temples,
begun by the architect, with many stages, and beflagged. It
would be unwise to piove by this that Bhasa innovated in these
regards; what is essential to Bana is to celebrate Bhasa’s fame,
